title: Integration, analytics & ML
oneLiner: SQS holds work for one worker, SNS pushes copies to many, EventBridge routes events (including SaaS and schedules). Data Streams keeps a stream for your own apps; Firehose just delivers it.

notes.html: Three ways to pass messages. Ask: does one worker pull it (queue), do many subscribers get a copy pushed (topic), or do events get routed by their content and source (bus)?

head: SQS
SNS
EventBridge
rows: Event bus, rules route events to targets
Your apps, AWS services, SaaS partners (Zendesk, Datadog, Salesforce…)

head: Also on the exam
Use it for
rows: Moving an existing RabbitMQ/ActiveMQ app that speaks AMQP, MQTT, STOMP. Don't rewrite to SQS
Orchestrating steps with retries and branches. Standard: up to 1 year, exactly-once. Express: up to 5 minutes, high volume
Copying data from SaaS apps (Salesforce, Zendesk) into S3 or Redshift on a schedule

items: "React to events from a SaaS app" → EventBridge partner event source. SQS and SNS have no SaaS sources.
"Copy SaaS data into S3 / Redshift" → AppFlow (data transfer), not EventBridge (events).
Fan-out where each consumer gets only some messages: SNS filter policies, not filtering in code.

notes.html: Data Streams stores the stream so your own apps can read and replay it. Firehose is a delivery truck: it buffers and drops the data in S3, Redshift or OpenSearch with no code.

notes.caption: Streams keeps data for consumers; Firehose delivers it

head: Kinesis Data Streams
Amazon Data Firehose
rows: Near real time (buffer by size or time; can be 0 s now)
Enhanced fan-out: 2 MB/s per consumer per shard
Converts JSON to Parquet/ORC on the way to S3

Each message goes to one worker and is deleted. No replay

items: "Custom application" / "multiple consumers" / "replay" → Data Streams. Firehose has no custom consumers.
"Easiest" / "no code" / "load into S3 or Redshift" → Firehose.
Several consumers falling behind on one stream → enhanced fan-out, not more Firehose.

notes.text: Throttle or buffer? API Gateway and Lambda

notes.html: Throttling rejects extra requests (HTTP 429). Buffering holds them until the backend catches up. Spiky load that must not be lost needs a buffer.

Make it async (SQS / Step Functions) and poll or notify

questions.q: A ride-sharing app sends GPS updates from thousands of cars. Three teams need to process the same stream with their own custom applications, and must be able to replay the last 24 hours after a bug fix. What should be used?

options.why: Firehose delivers to destinations. No custom consumers, no replay.
Right. Stored records, many custom consumers, replay within retention.
Each message goes to one consumer and is deleted after processing.
No storage, so no replay.

questions.q: A company wants clickstream data loaded into S3 in Parquet format for Athena, with the least operational overhead and no custom code. What should they use?

options.t: Kinesis Data Streams with a KCL consumer that writes Parquet
options.why: Works, but you write and run the consumer.

options.t: Amazon Data Firehose with format conversion to Parquet
options.why: Right. Fully managed delivery with built-in conversion.

options.t: SQS with Lambda writing to S3
options.why: Custom code, and Lambda would need to batch and convert.
A message broker for legacy protocols.

questions.q: Four consumer applications read from one Kinesis data stream and are falling behind because they share the read throughput of each shard. What fixes this with the least change?

options.why: Firehose doesn't support custom consumers.

options.t: Enable enhanced fan-out for the consumers
options.why: Right. Each consumer gets its own 2 MB/s per shard, pushed.
Retention doesn't add read throughput.

options.t: Put an SQS queue in front
options.why: Changes the design and loses multi-consumer reads.

questions.q: Logs must reach Amazon OpenSearch Service within about a minute. A small Lambda function must mask emails first. The team wants a managed service with no servers. What fits best?

options.t: Firehose with a Lambda transformation, delivering to OpenSearch
options.why: Right. Near real-time delivery with a built-in transform hook.

options.t: Kinesis Data Streams with consumers on EC2
options.why: Servers to manage.
No delivery to OpenSearch, and FIFO isn't needed.
For schedules, not log streams.

questions.q: Firehose is delivering to S3 with a 60-second buffer. A dashboard needs data sooner, but the team doesn't want to manage consumers. What is true?

options.t: 60 seconds is the minimum, so they must switch to Data Streams
options.why: The minimum used to be 60 s. Firehose buffer intervals can now be set as low as 0 s.

options.t: They can lower the buffer interval, down to 0 seconds
options.why: Right. Firehose is still described as near real time on the exam.

options.t: Firehose delivers in real time by default
options.why: It buffers by size or time.
SQS doesn't deliver to S3.

questions.q: Support tickets created in Zendesk must trigger a Lambda function in AWS. What is the most direct way to receive these events?

options.t: An SQS queue subscribed to Zendesk
options.why: SQS has no SaaS partner sources.

options.t: An SNS topic that Zendesk publishes to
options.why: SNS has no native SaaS partner integration.

options.t: An EventBridge partner event source and a rule targeting Lambda
options.why: Right. Zendesk is a SaaS partner; events arrive on a partner event bus.
AppFlow copies data in batches; it doesn't route events to Lambda.

questions.q: Every night at 02:00 a Lambda function must start a cleanup job. What is the simplest serverless way to schedule it?

options.t: A cron job on an EC2 instance
options.why: A server to run and patch.

options.t: EventBridge Scheduler (or a scheduled EventBridge rule)
options.why: Right. Serverless cron that invokes Lambda.
Max delay is 15 minutes.
SNS has no schedules.

questions.q: An order service publishes events. The billing, shipping and analytics services each need every order, and each must be able to process at its own pace even if it is down for an hour. What is the best design?

options.t: One SQS queue read by all three
options.why: Each message is delivered to only one of them.

options.t: SNS topic fanning out to three SQS queues
options.why: Right. Every service gets a copy and its own queue as a buffer.

options.t: SNS topic with three Lambda subscribers
options.why: No buffer if a consumer is down for an hour.

options.t: Three direct API calls from the order service
options.why: Tight coupling, and failures need custom retries.

questions.q: An SNS topic fans out to several SQS queues. The refunds queue should only receive messages where type = "refund". How should this be done with the least effort?

options.t: Filter in the refunds consumer and drop the rest
options.why: Works, but wastes processing and cost.

options.t: Add a subscription filter policy on the refunds queue's subscription
options.why: Right. SNS only delivers matching messages.

options.t: Create a separate topic per type
options.why: More topics and publisher changes.
Order isn't the problem.

questions.q: Workers sometimes process the same SQS message twice. Processing takes about 2 minutes. What is the most likely cause?

options.why: Delay only affects first delivery.

options.t: The visibility timeout (30 s) is shorter than the processing time
options.why: Right. The message reappears before the worker deletes it.
Long polling doesn't cause duplicates.

options.t: The retention period is too short
options.why: That would lose messages, not duplicate them.

questions.q: An e-commerce app must process each customer's order events in order, but different customers' events should be processed in parallel. What should be used?

options.why: No ordering guarantee.

options.t: SQS FIFO queue with the customer ID as the message group ID
options.why: Right. Ordered per group, parallel across groups.

options.t: SQS FIFO queue with one message group ID for everything
options.why: Strict order, but only one at a time.
No ordering guarantee.

questions.q: An application must send 5 MB documents through SQS. What should the architect do?

options.t: Raise the queue's maximum message size to 5 MB
options.why: The limit is 1 MiB (it was 256 KB until 2025).

options.t: Use the SQS Extended Client Library to store the payload in S3 and send a pointer
options.why: Right. The standard pattern for large payloads.
SNS has the same kind of size limit.

options.t: Split each document into many messages without tracking
options.why: Reassembly and ordering become your problem.

questions.q: A public REST API sometimes gets 10x traffic spikes that overwhelm the backend workers. No requests may be lost. What should the architect add?

options.why: Throttling rejects requests with 429, so they're lost unless clients retry.

options.t: An SQS queue between API Gateway and the workers
options.why: Right. The queue buffers the spike and workers catch up.

options.t: SNS between API Gateway and the workers
options.why: SNS pushes right away and doesn't buffer.
Doesn't absorb a spike.

questions.q: A report endpoint behind API Gateway sometimes takes 2 minutes to finish. Clients get timeouts. What is the best design?

options.t: Raise the Lambda timeout to 15 minutes
options.why: API Gateway still times out at 29 s by default.

options.t: Make it asynchronous: accept the request, queue the work (SQS or Step Functions), and let clients poll or get notified
options.why: Right. The classic exam answer for long work behind an API.

options.t: Increase the API Gateway integration timeout for all API types
options.why: Only Regional/private REST APIs can request a higher limit now, and the exam answer is still 29 s + async.
Changes the front door but not the design problem.

questions.q: A SaaS company sells API access. Each customer must have its own request quota and rate limit. What should be used?

options.t: API Gateway usage plans with API keys
options.why: Right. Per-customer throttling and quotas.
Rate-limits by IP, not by customer plan.
Doesn't limit request rates.
Not tied to customer identity.

questions.q: A company runs an on-premises app that uses ActiveMQ with the AMQP protocol and wants to move it to AWS without code changes. What should they use?

options.why: Would need code changes; SQS doesn't speak AMQP.
Right. Managed ActiveMQ/RabbitMQ with standard protocols.
Different model and API.
Different model and API.

questions.q: An analyst runs Athena queries on CSV logs in S3 and the bill is high. Which TWO changes cut cost the most?

options.why: Right. Columnar: Athena reads only the columns a query needs.

options.t: Partition the data by date and filter on it
options.why: Right. Athena skips partitions it doesn't need.
Athena reads S3.
Helps a little, but the big wins are columnar format and partitions.

options.t: Run queries from an EC2 instance
options.why: Athena is serverless; that changes nothing.

questions.q: A company keeps 2 years of hot data in Redshift and 8 years of history in S3. Analysts must join both in single queries without loading the history into Redshift. What should they use?

options.why: Can query S3, but not join with Redshift tables in one query.
Right. Redshift queries S3 data in place and joins it.
Possible, but heavier and not Redshift.
They catalog data; they don't run the query.

questions.q: A bank must process scanned loan applications: extract form fields, detect personal information in the text, and send low-confidence results to people for review. Which combination fits?

options.why: Rekognition is for images and faces, not form fields.
Right. Extract, analyze text for PII, human review.
Those handle audio.
Search, recommendations and generative AI.

questions.q: A retailer wants demand forecasts from 3 years of daily sales data. The question offers these options. Which is the expected answer on older exam questions, and what should a new project use today?

options.t: Amazon Forecast on the exam; SageMaker (e.g., Canvas) for a new project
options.why: Right. Forecast closed to new customers in 2024, but older questions still use it.
Personalize is for recommendations.
Comprehend analyzes text.
A warehouse stores data; it doesn't forecast.

questions.q: An app must send order confirmation emails and track bounces, with the least operational overhead.

options.why: Managed email sending with bounce and complaint tracking.
For simple notifications to subscribers, not customer email at scale.
Servers and reputation to manage.
A queue, not email delivery.

questions.q: A small team wants to host a React front end with a serverless backend and auto-deploy on every Git push, with the least setup.

options.why: Built-in CI/CD from Git plus hosting.
Works, but more to build.
Server-based app environments.
Servers to manage.
